original_value: Along with the increasing popularity of larval zebrafish as an experimental animal in the fields of drug screening, neuroscience, genetics, and developmental biology, the need for tools to deal with multiple larvae has emerged. Microfluidic channels have been employed to handle multiple larvae simultaneously, even for sensing electroencephalogram (EEG). In this study, we developed a microfluidic chip capable of uniform and continuous drug infusion across all microfluidic channels during EEG recording. Owing to the modular design of the microfluidic channels, the number of animals under investigation can be easily increased. Using the optimized design of the microfluidic chip, liquids could be exchanged uniformly across all channels without physically affecting the larvae contained in the channels, which assured a stable environment maintained all the time during EEG recording, by eliminating environmental artifacts and leaving only biological effects to be seen. To demonstrate the usefulness of the developed system in drug screening, we continuously measured EEG from four larvae without and with pentylenetetrazole application, up to 60 min. In addition, we recorded EEG from valproic acid (VPA)-treated zebrafish and demonstrated the suppression of seizure by VPA. The developed microfluidic system could contribute to the mass screening of EEG for drug development to treat neurological disorders such as epilepsy in a short time, owing to its handy size, cheap fabrication cost, and the guaranteed uniform drug infusion across all channels with no environmentally induced artifacts.

result.paraphrase: As larval zebrafish have become increasingly popular experimental animals in drug screening, neuroscience, genetics, and developmental biology, tools for managing multiple larvae have been needed. Microfluidic channels have been used to handle several larvae at once, including for electroencephalogram (EEG) sensing. Here, we developed a microfluidic chip that enables uniform, continuous drug infusion through all microfluidic channels during EEG recording. Because the microfluidic channels are modularly designed, the number of animals being studied can be readily expanded. With the optimized chip design, liquids could be exchanged evenly across all channels without physically disturbing the larvae inside, ensuring a stable recording environment at all times by removing environmental artifacts and leaving only biological effects. To show the system’s value for drug screening, we continuously recorded EEG from four larvae with and without pentylenetetrazole for up to 60 min. We also recorded EEG from valproic acid (VPA)-treated zebrafish and showed VPA suppressed seizures. Owing to its compact size, low fabrication cost, and guaranteed uniform drug infusion across all channels without environmentally induced artifacts, the developed microfluidic system may help enable rapid, large-scale EEG screening for drug development against neurological disorders such as epilepsy.
